canberra.title: Teenager accused of forcibly confining ex-partner, hitting her with a pool cue refused bail
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article discusses allegations of family and domestic violence. An 18-year-old man’s been accused of forcibly ...
canberra.content:
A Lyons man fronted ACT Magistrates Court on Monday (2 November), accused of several offences against his ex-partner. Photo: John Lomnicki.

CONTENT WARNING: This article discusses allegations of family and domestic violence.

An 18-year-old man’s been accused of forcibly confining his ex-partner and hitting her with a pool cue as part of allegations described by a special magistrate as putting her “at great risk of life and limb”.

The Lyons man, whom Region has not named to protect the identity of the complainant, was charged with two counts of aggravated common assault and one count each of forcible confinement, aggravated damage to property, chokes/suffocates/strangles another person, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and threatening to distribute intimate images when he appeared in the ACT Magistrates Court on Monday (2 November).

It’s alleged an argument broke out between the pair at a Lyons home on Saturday (31 October).

Special Magistrate Michael Cowen read out the allegations, which included that the man threatened to “post nude images” of the woman on TikTok if she tried to leave the premises.

It’s alleged the fight escalated to the point where the man hit the woman on the arm three times with a pool cue.

“She described the pain as 8 out of 10; her arm was throbbing,” Special Magistrate Cowen read.

“She began crying; he began mocking her – ‘oh look, now you’re the victim’.”

It’s alleged the man hit her again with the pool cue across the hand and threatened that, if he punched her “with full force … [she] would die”.

The man’s also accused of placing his hands over the complainant’s mouth to the point where she had trouble breathing.

During the bail application, the man’s defence lawyer argued bail conditions could address any risk of offending, and would protect the safety and welfare of the complainant.

He submitted conditions could be imposed so that the accused would “essentially [be] on house arrest” with his parents, and there wouldn’t be a risk of the complainant and accused coming into contact as they “broke up some months ago”.

“It is clear that she does not intend to engage with him further,” the defence submitted.

“Preventative detention should not be a path taken.”

Prosecutor Garth Morrison disagreed, submitting the alleged offending was “quite serious”.

“It begins with a threat to share intimate photos with not just anybody but potentially with everybody,” he submitted.

“And from there, it escalates for a period of almost two hours.”

Mr Morrison submitted the alleged incident “must have been a significant and scary time” for the complainant, and that she “remains fearful”.

“She feels weak and vulnerable and now, due to her injuries, has just one arm to defend herself,” he said.

Mr Morrison described photos of the complainant’s alleged injuries to the court, which he submitted included evidence of lacerations, swelling and a potentially fractured bone.

Special Magistrate Cowen said the complainant was “clearly vitally injured” in the photos, and that the alleged offending was “prolonged, involving weapons, [with the] very, very concerning restriction of the ability to breathe”.

He determined the allegedly prolonged “violence [which was] cruel at times [and posed] great risk of life and limb” meant he wasn’t satisfied that bail was appropriate.

The man is scheduled to re-appear in court on 23 November.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero (000).

canberra.title: Access Canberra ticks off Big Splash’s makeshift ‘restaurant’ despite packing up shop in less than a day
canberra.snippet: Access Canberra has confirmed Big Splash’s 24-hour, makeshift ‘family restaurant’ complied with the reopening condition...
canberra.content:
Locked up and locked out, Big Splash’s family restaurant has already packed up after a single day of trading out front of the boarded-up water park, leaving many, including Amelia Tattam, angry and confused. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Access Canberra has confirmed Big Splash’s 24-hour, makeshift ‘family restaurant’ complied with the reopening conditions of its crown lease, despite many labelling it a barbecue in disguise.

The waterpark, which is now 20 years into a 99-year crownland lease, was bought by Translink Management Group in 2021 for $7.5 million but closed its doors just two years later, in late 2023.

The site has had several orders to reopen since its closure, one in November 2025 and more recently on 1 November 2026, with the site’s regulator, Access Canberra, threatening to terminate the lease if the lessees were non-compliant.

Although the site failed to reopen in 2025, with the owners blaming rising renovation costs, Access Canberra was satisfied work was underway to reopen the park.

In June 2026, Big Splash was listed for sale. Despite still being on the market, Big Splash was still required to open in some capacity by 1 November.

Big Splash technically met its 1 November lease requirements by opening what it labelled an unlicensed family restaurant at the park’s entry. However, those who visited the park on Sunday were greeted with a small marquee, a barbecue and a portable toilet.

Not even a day later, the temporary set-up had been packed up.

All that remains from Big Splash’s family restaurant are some chairs and a portable toilet. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Amelia Tattam, who has been leading the Save Big Splash campaign, was left mortified by Big Splash’s reopening, calling the event a box-ticking exercise for owners to keep the lease.

“When I arrived on Sunday, there was a little food tent set up. Not quite the restaurant we were promised,” she said.

“We were told there was going to be a restaurant after they knew they weren’t going to open the park by 1 November. Now, not even a day after it opened, it’s gone.

“To call it a restaurant is quite generous, especially given the other cafes and shops around the Jamison Centre. It just felt like a way to tick a box so they can keep a hold of the lease a little longer.”

A QR code linking to a frequently asked questions website has been hung on the front gate of the park. The site was last updated in July 2026. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Despite the disappointment of Ms Tattam and others hoping for the park’s reopening, Access Canberra has given the barbecue the tick of approval, saying it considered the lessee compliant with its lease conditions.

“The Crown lease does not define the term ‘unlicensed family restaurant’ or prescribe a particular building type, operating model, scale or minimum frequency of operation,” an Access Canberra spokesperson said.

“We recognise that this outcome may not meet the expectations of members of the community who want to see Big Splash restored as a water park. There has been significant community interest in the future of the site. However, the role of the regulator is to apply the law as it stands, based on the facts and circumstances of each individual matter.

“Regulatory action cannot be taken simply because a different outcome may be preferred and where there are not reasonable prospects of success of litigation.

“The Crown lease permits the site to be used for an aquatic facility, an indoor sports facility or an unlicensed family restaurant. Access Canberra’s role is therefore to determine whether the use of the land complies with the lease and relevant legislation, rather than to determine which permitted use should be pursued.

“There are no current regulatory matters in progress relating to this lease.”

Member for Ginninderra and Liberal MLA Peter Cain has slammed the ‘reopening’, calling the situation an embarrassing farce for the ACT Government.

“Canberrans were promised a swimming pool. Instead, they got a BBQ masquerading as an ‘unlicensed family restaurant’, and even that couldn’t last 24 hours,” he said.

“The government has known about these problems for well over a year. It threatened lease enforcement, granted extensions and accepted assurances, yet delivered nothing for Canberra’s families.

“If the government knew the lease allowed a restaurant instead of a waterpark, why did it spend months promising a Big Splash pool would open from the 1st of November? Either it misunderstood its own lease or made promises it couldn’t enforce.

“Neither is acceptable.”

It is unclear whether the restaurant will return in the future.

canberra.title: Canavan to fight One Nation in Lower House seat, but it won’t be Hanson’s ‘right-hand man’
canberra.snippet: Nationals leader Matt Canavan has done what everyone knew he would do, confirming he will make a tilt for a seat in the Lower House of Fe...
canberra.content:
Nationals Leader Matt Canavan has confirmed he will run for a seat in the House of Representatives. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan has done what everyone knew he would do, confirming he will make a tilt for a seat in the Lower House of Federal Parliament.

A successful switch from the Senate, where he now sits, to the House of Representatives would put him in a prime position to be deputy prime minister – if the Coalition can win the next election, that is.

Senator Canavan confirmed on Monday (2 November) that he will nominate for the federal Queensland seat of Capricornia, currently held by fellow National Michelle Landry.

Ms Landry, the Nationals’ Chief Whip, recently announced she will retire at the next federal election, which is due in 2028. That announcement sparked instant speculation that Senator Canavan would seek preselection for the seat.

The speculation was right.

“With Michelle announcing her retirement, someone’s got to step up and, effectively, I’m the next person up here in Central Queensland,” he said on Monday.

“Who knows, I might not be successful. But I’m not going to die wondering … In the Lower House, you go [to a federal election] every three years, you’ve got to come up for a performance review.

“So I’m hungry for it. I’m young and got the energy for it.

“I’ll just be out there fighting for it every day. And I’ll live and die by the judgment of central Queensland.

“It’s their choice … there’s no safe seats anymore.”

If Senator Canavan wins Nationals preselection for Capricornia, he will have to quit the Senate when the next election is called.

His Senate term expires at the next election, and he would have had to contest his re-election for that seat.

Ms Landry was standing with Senator Canavan when he announced his decision in Rockhampton on Monday.

She (unsurprisingly) gave him her full endorsement.

“It’s a big job doing this, and I think Matt’s certainly up for it,” she said.

Senator Canavan said he would have loved Ms Landry, who has held the seat since 2013, to run again because she is “as close to a sure thing as” the Nationals could have there.

But he is not prepared to let One Nation take the seat without a fight.

“I’m happy to put my political future on the line to deliver that, to take our country back,” he said.

One Nation’s controversial national director James Ashby has ruled himself out of the contest, confirming by statement on Monday (2 November) that he will not run for the seat.

“I’ll play a role in the campaign here in Capricornia, but my position as national director is one that I take seriously; therefore, I won’t be nominating at preselection,” he said.

“I know of a number of very worthy contenders here in Capricornia who I’ll be encouraging to put their hand up when nominations open.

“Capricornia is a seat One Nation can win, so I intend to throw the resources and people behind a strong campaign.”

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has also ruled out running for the seat, which would also require her to leave the Senate.

“Am I running in Capricornia? No, I’m not running in Capricornia, so I’ll give you a direct answer to that one,” she said when asked by the media in Melbourne on Monday.

“What Matt Canavan does is Matt Canavan’s choice to do what he wants to do, but it’s not my choice to run in Capricornia.”

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has voiced his support for Senator Canavan’s decision.

“He’s putting it all on the line,” Mr Taylor said.

“We’re all putting it all on the line because we have to, because we need our country back.”

Ms Landry holds Capricornia for the Nationals on a margin of 5.8 per cent, after a slight swing to Labor at the last election.

Over the years, the Nationals have fought off Labor with varying levels of success — fluctuating from hyper-marginal results to a safe seat and everything in between.

Ms Landry has won five consecutive terms, and in normal times, Capricornia could be considered a safe bet for a Nationals candidate to win another – “normal times” being the key phrase here.

canberra.title: Lake Burley Griffin’s new rowing arena open just in time for Australia’s premier rowing festival
canberra.snippet: Red Shed has officially delivered Lake Burley Griffin’s newest lakeside venue just in time for Canberra’s biggest rowing comp...
canberra.content:
ACT Minister for Sport Chris Steel and Red Shed President John Gasson officially opened the new waterfront amphitheatre on the Lake Burley Griffin Peninsula. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Red Shed has officially delivered Lake Burley Griffin’s newest lakeside venue just in time for Canberra’s biggest rowing competition, The Golden Oar Regatta Festival.

The $1 million Canberra Coastal Rowing Arena at Black Mountain Peninsula has officially opened only three months after its DA was approved.

The new venue is Australia’s first-ever purpose-built lake arena for coastal rowing and beach sprints, which will make its Olympic debut at Los Angeles in 2028.

Red Shed founder and president John Gasson said the opening represented an important milestone not just for rowing, but for Canberra.

“This started with an ambition to create something special for coastal rowing, but it has become much bigger than that,” Mr Gasson said.

“We now have a beautiful new public space on the shores of Lake Burley Griffin that can be used for everything from sport and community activity to concerts, theatre, markets and events.

“There could hardly be a better way to open it than by welcoming some of the best rowers in the world to Canberra.”

A view of the new amphitheatre on the Lake Burley Griffin peninsula. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

One of the first two rowers to use the new venue and a bronze medalist at the World Rowing Beach Sprint Finals campaign in China, Catherine Khan, said having a facility where coastal rowers can now train in the ACT firmly cements Canberra as the country’s rowing capital.

“In the past, when we’ve practised sprint rowing, we’ve run off a pontoon,” Ms Khan said.

“Having a location in Canberra where we can now properly practise entries and exits is amazing.

“In the lead-up to the World Championships and Olympic qualifiers in 2027, we will use this arena three to four times a week to practise entries and exits.

“It’s a massive game changer, and it means we can now do most of our training in Canberra.”

Canberra Airport’s CEO Stephen Byron helping the athletes with their equipment. Photos: Brad Redfern.

Teams putting their final touches on their boats.

Winners are grinners

Rowers from around the world having a laugh.

The new rowing arena and amphitheatre came just in time for Canberrans to cheer on the world’s best rowers at the Golden Oar Regatta, which returned for its second year.

More than $200,000 in prize money was on offer across the three-day event, making the Golden Oar one of the richest events in international rowing.

Mr Gasson said the strength of the field, which included reigning world champions in the women’s double sculls, Romanian stars Simona Radiș and Adriana Adam and three-time Olympic gold medallists, Croatian brothers Martin and Valent Sinković, demonstrated how quickly the Golden Oar had established itself.

The Australian Rowing team (The Rowsellas) were popular with spectators. Photos: Brad Redfern/Red Shed.

Teams from across the world including Germany travelled to Canberra for the Golden Oar.

The Dutch rowing team.

Multiple disciplines including the Mixed Coxed Eight were held over the weekend event.

The Red Shed president said he was thrilled with the turnout of the event over the weekend, believing the quality of talent led to the huge attendance.

“To have had this calibre of athlete racing together in Australia is extraordinarily rare,” he said.

“We had Olympic champions, current world champions and some of the biggest names in rowing coming to Canberra to race against one another.

“For Australian rowing fans, it was a field you would normally have to travel to an Olympic Games or World Championships to see. For everyone else, we deliberately created an event where you don’t need to know anything about rowing to have a great day out.”

To view the festival results, visit Golden Oar.

canberra.title: Vinyl Record Fair community day to help food pantry feed Canberrans
canberra.snippet: Since when does buying vinyl records help a local charity feed Canberrans in need? When those records are bought at the inaugural Vinyl R...
canberra.content:
Rob Pash, of newly named Pashing Vinyl, has thinned out his own collection to sell at the Vinyl Record Fair in Griffith. Photo: Region.

Since when does buying vinyl records help a local charity feed Canberrans in need?

When those records are bought at the inaugural Vinyl Record Fair in Griffith, right next to the Griffith Shops, that’s when.

Community Services #1 Food Pantry is hosting a record fair in the Griffith Neighbourhood Hall on Sunday, 8 November, bringing together music collectors, vendors and enthusiasts from across the ACT.

Entry is free, but the local stallholders are all contributing to Community Services #1 (CS#1) to go towards its most worthy causes.

A barbecue throughout the day, along with other activities and promotions, will also help raise funds at what organisers are planning to be a fun, family friendly, community event.

The CS#1 food pantry is a community outlet for people with a genuine need or those on a limited income.

It makes good food affordable and accessible, with the food being provided by FoodBank NSW, OzHarvest, The Period Project and community donations.

In 2025-26 the pantry had roughly 3200 pantry visits and provided support to about 240 community members.

There were 94 emergency hampers supplied over that period; assistance given to 166 individuals and families through the Christmas support program; and 10 back-to-school packs for local students.

“We are delighted that the organisers of the Vinyl Record Fair are supporting Community Services #1 through this event,” the organisation’s chief executive officer Simon Bennett said.

“All funds raised for CS#1 will go to our Community Food Pantry in Narrabundah, which continues to experience high levels of demand.”

In addition to vinyl records, CDs, and DVDs on sale throughout the day, there will also be plenty of collectibles and curiosities up for grabs.; as well as some very well-priced hifi equipment.

In other words – something for everyone.

And it won’t be the usual vendors seen at record markets around town. They’re all local and some haven’t sold records at fairs before.

One such seller is Rob Pash, who will be calling his stand Pashing Vinyl.

“Don’t take my name in vain,” he laughed.

“That was a bit of fun on the side when I was setting up a payment app and it forced me to choose a business name, which I’d never even considered at all. I came up with that on the fly and it will have to do.”

Pash isn’t a professional seller, he’s just clearing out some of his own collection and jumped at the chance to be part of a community event.

His immaculately kept records span genres and eras, with some quite rare specimens for sale.

“I’m not a collector, I’m an accumulator,” he said.

“I’ve been buying long players since I was about 12.

“If record storage takes over any more of our living space at home, I can reasonably expect divorce papers to be in the mail shortly. [laughs all round].

“I just have to think about moving some records on, and a community event like this is a really fantastic way of doing that – connecting with people; connecting with the community.

“It is very, very hard to give up a lot of them, but I’m in my mid 50s and I have to be realistic about what I’m listening to these days and, you know, tastes change over time.

“Bands, artists come and go; you fall in and out of love with them and that’s a really great part of the journey too.”

Pashing Vinyl’s prices range from surprisingly great bargains to those with somewhat higher price tags on rare albums – but even those are bargains compared to what some are selling for online.

“It was an onerous task pricing them,” he said.

“I had no idea what some of them could be worth, but I had to be as realistic about the prices as I was about thinning out the collection.

“There’s something there for everybody – it’s a very eclectic mix of records.”

Griffith Neighbourhood Hall will transform into a Vinyl Record Fair on Sunday, 8 November. Photo: Region.

Canberra’s Kool N’ Krazy Records will be there also, specialising in Afro-American LPs, soul, funk, jazz, blues and RnB.

Black Velvet Records will also be there, headed by Tom Stokman who has had record stores in Kingston and Bungendore over the years.

That’s a just a small sample of the numerous stallholders who will be at the fair, which is set to be a fun day just a few steps away from the Griffiths Shops.

The Vinyl Record Fair Day is on Sunday 8 November from 10 am to 3 pm at the Griffith Neighbourhood Hall. Entry is free.

australia.title: Ashanti: ‘I’ve had a bodysuit snap off on stage. That was not my coolest moment’
australia.snippet: Ahead of her Australian tour, the Grammy winner talks about her marriage to Nelly, fans rushing the stage and her secret skill Get our we...
australia.content:
Your debut album Ashanti turns 25 next year and you’re in the process of re-recording it. How do you feel about that album now?

We are rerecording it so I will own my masters. Sonically, it will be a lot clearer. It was 25 years ago so it’ll sound a little more new, obviously, but with the same classic vibe. I’m very excited. What I’ve learned is that I’m just really grateful to have written records that stand the test of time. Foolish is turning 25! That I can still go to an arena and hold the mic in the air and hear everyone sing those lyrics is a beautiful feeling. And a blessing.

Owning my masters is really important to me. Nowadays, obviously, things are a lot different compared with back when I first came out as an artist. But after 20 years, you get the right to go in and legally rerecord your masters … and take back what’s yours, so to speak. Hopefully it inspires artists to try and take control from the beginning – hopefully you don’t have to wait 20 years! But if you do, you go in, you get it done and you have fun with it.

You and your husband, Nelly, have been together for decades. What do you like most about him and what gets on your nerves?

He has got to have the biggest heart I know. He is so generous and genuine – he will literally take the shirt off of his back and give it to you. He’s really a beautiful person. And he taught me a lot about staying positive and looking at the glass half full, as opposed to half empty. He has an amazing heart.

What gets on my nerves? Definitely the thermostat. He likes it to be cold and I like it to be warm and toasty and cozy. A lot of our beef happens over the thermostat. Our compromise number is 70 degrees fahrenheit (21C) because I would prefer 80, 85 and he would prefer, like, 60. I’m like, “Bro, come on!” So we agreed on 70.

What has been your most memorable interaction with a fan?

Obviously 20 years ago it was very different – you are a new artist so people would come up to me, crying and shaking. And I’m very grateful for that. But being in the game for 20-plus years, teenagers that weren’t even born back then come up to me now. I met a young girl recently and I was like “How do you even know Foolish?” I saw her singing every word in the audience with her mom. It was the coolest thing.

  • Sign up for the fun stuff with our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morning

You want to hear something crazy? This young girl did an interview with me at SiriusXM recently and she said, “Oh my god, I love you! My dad named me after you!”

As a millennial, John Tucker Must Die is a very important film to me. Do you find acting easy? How does it compare to making music?

It’s just another muscle to flex. I really enjoy acting. I think the difference is you have a lot more control in music, especially if you write your own music. If you’re on stage, you know people are there to see you. When you’re acting, you’re portraying a character that someone else has written and you’re being directed … so although it’s really cool to dip into another version of yourself, it’s kind of limiting because you’re there to portray what they want you to.

What’s the most chaotic thing that’s ever happened to you on stage?

I definitely have had some – I guess we’re going to call them very excited fans – jump on stage and give me a hug mid-performance. I’ve also had a bodysuit snap off on stage. That was not my coolest moment. We had to have the band play for a second. I went into the wing and got it together.

When you get to a hotel, what’s the first thing you do?

I wipe down the phone and the remote with disinfectant wipes – always!

If you could collaborate with another artist you haven’t already worked with, who would it be and why?

I like a lot of the newer R&B girls; they are really cool. I love SZA, I think she’s really, really dope. She’s shown me so much love since the beginning. Summer Walker is dope too. And I like women empowerment. Nothing against the guys!

What is the best lesson you’ve learned from someone that you’ve worked with?

Usually your gut is right. Sometimes, as artists, we second guess ourselves – but usually your gut is right and you’ve got to follow it. My husband has definitely said that to me, because he’s always like, “You second guess yourself!” But we all do that.

Is your baby boy coming along on the Australia tour?

Yes, he’s coming to Australia with me. I really thought long and hard about it but I can’t go that long without seeing him. I’m very grateful and blessed to have an amazing nanny. It definitely takes a village. Being a working mom and travelling all over the world definitely takes its toll. And I’m a mom that cooks all of his food from scratch. Everything is organic. Most people have liquor, chips, candy on their rider – and mine is just like, organic sweet potatoes!

What are you secretly really good at?

I don’t know if it’s a secret, but I’m actually a really good cook. My go-to dish is Chilean sea bass with rice and vegetables. And I am good at impressions.

Who’s your best impression?

[In a very convincing Australian accent] Well, I think my best imitation might be you at the moment.

  • Ashanti’s Australian tour kicks off in Perth on 9 November

australia.title: Guardian Essential poll: record number of Australians are turning their backs on the Melbourne Cup
australia.snippet: Growing disdain for gambling and animal cruelty concerns drive sliding interest in race that once ‘stopped the nation’ Get our breaking n...
australia.content:
A record number of Australians are turning their backs on the Melbourne Cup, with more than two-thirds surveyed saying they have low or zero interest in the annual horse race.

Support for the Melbourne Cup has been sliding consistently for a number of years, but the Guardian Essential poll found just 9% of Australians said they had high interest in the race now – nearly half the proportion in 2025.

“The race that once stopped the nation is now just white noise for many,” Peter Lewis, chair of Essential Media, said.

The Guardian Essential poll of 1,003 Australians in late October highlights the latest erosion in popularity of the event amid growing ambivalence to the event.

Just 9% of people said they had high interest in the Cup, down 7 percentage points from 2025, with another 23% professing moderate interest, also down 3 points. About 29% of voters said they had low interest (up 5 points from last year), while another 39% said no interest at all (up 8 points).

The combined high and moderate interest came to only 32%, the lowest on record since Essential began asking this question in annual polling in November 2022. The combined low and no interest vote was 68%, jumping 12 points from last year to its highest on record.

In November 2022, the low and no interest vote came to a combined 52%; it was 62% in 2023, 52% in 2024, and 56% in 2025.

The “nup to the Cup” movement, backed by some high-profile politicians and celebrities, has contributed to declining support for the race.

But 62% of Australians nonetheless agreed the Melbourne Cup was a unique part of Australia’s national identity. That number remains a strong majority view, despite falling from 78% agreement when Essential asked this question in 2019.

Half of Australians (50%) believe the Cup promotes unhealthy gambling behaviour, up 3% since 2025, while 36% say they feel the Cup normalises animal cruelty, down 3 points from 2025.

Another 48% said they were less interested in the Cup than they used to be.

“The key driver appears to be a growing disdain for gambling, although concern for animal cruelty comes a close second,” Lewis said.

“More broadly this reflects the decline in unifying atonal moments in a world where more and more people have their experiences mediated by targeted advertising algorithms.”

Just 12% of voters in October’s poll said they regularly wagered on horse races and would bet on Tuesday’s Melbourne Cup, down 5 points from 2025. In contrast, 46% of people said they were not interested in the Cup and would not place a bet, up 6 points from last year.

Another 25% said they rarely bet on horses but would watch the race and place a bet, while 17% said they would watch but not bet.

australia.title: Reddit and libertarian group challenge Australia’s under-16s social media ban in high court
australia.snippet: Social network and Digital Freedom Project, led by NSW state MP John Ruddick, seek to overturn ban on grounds of implied freedom of polit...
australia.content:
Australia’s world-leading under-16s social media ban will face its first major legal challenge on Tuesday, as Reddit and an advocacy group headed by a libertarian politician seek to overturn the law in the high court.

Nearly 11 months ago, 10 platforms – Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, Kick, X, Twitch and Threads – were required to deactivate or suspend the accounts of users they determined to be aged under 16 years.

Since then, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has said more than 5m accounts across the 10 services have been suspended as part of the ban.

Whether the ban will stay will be the subject of the high court hearings on Tuesday and Wednesday this week as Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project – led by New South Wales state Libertarian MP John Ruddick – seek to overturn the ban.

Australia does not have a guaranteed right to freedom of speech, and the case largely focuses on whether preventing under-16s from holding a social media account impermissibly burdens the implied freedom of political communication in Australian law.

Reddit has argued in its submission to the court that online platforms are a “common source of news and political information” in Australia. The company pointed to its “Ask Me Anything” sessions on the site where users have historically asked questions of politicians of candidates.

Teens, Reddit said, would not be able to make posts on politics, comment or react to political content, or engage with the social media accounts of the youth wings of the major political parties.

The Australian government has argued in its defence that the law serves the legitimate purposes of seeking to reduce the risk of harm for under-16s from social media platforms for the “harmful features” including algorithms, infinite scroll, persistent notifications and likes.

While the Digital Freedom Project adopted many of the same arguments on political communications burden as Reddit in its submission, the group is likely to face an additional hurdle with the government challenging the standing of the group to bring the case to the court.

Digital Freedom Group had initially had two teens – Noah Jones and Macey Nyland – as the original lead plaintiffs for the case as teens affected by the ban. However in July both were withdrawn from the case, leaving it to the advocacy group.

It is understood there was concerns that the teens would face potential legal costs against them in the event of a loss.

Digital Freedom Project has argued in its submission that some of its members are between the ages of 13 and 15, and the teens are likely to be presented as examples in the case, but the federal government has argued that as the plaintiff, Digital Freedom Project does not have standing to bring the case.

The federal government’s submission argues the group has not identified any activity of the group that is impeded by the ban.

Legal experts have been divided on the prospect of success. The constitutional law expert Prof Anne Twomey wrote last year that Reddit could be successful in highlighting the mismatch between the intended purpose of the law and the practical effect – if the restriction is not preventing children from the harms while also restricting their freedom of political communication.

Luke Beck, professor of constitutional law at Monash University, wrote in the Guardian last year the cases were likely to fail, as the social media account ban only slightly reduces the overall volume of political communication in Australia, and 13-, 14- and 15-year-olds were not engaging in much political communication before the ban.

Beck said last week the extra hurdle for Digital Freedom Project to prove standing would also be difficult.

“The government is arguing that DFP is not impacted by the law so therefore can’t challenge it,” he said. “We’ll see what the high court says about advocacy groups having standing to challenge laws: traditionally the courts aren’t too keen.”

Many other countries are considering following Australia’s lead, but there have been concerns teens have been able to easily circumvent the ban. The federal opposition has also raised concerns that the number of accounts suspended may be inflated, while the government has refused to release numbers broken down by platform.

As the legal challengers get their day in court, the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, is also using new powers passed by parliament this year to investigate whether TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Instagram and Facebook are in compliance with the law, given the number of teens still holding accounts.

The companies could be facing the prospect of fines of up to nearly $100m a breach, if the regulator decides to take the case to the federal court.

The federal parliament is also debating the digital duty of care legislation mandating platforms take actions to prevent users experiencing harm on their platforms. Beck has said the passage of this legislation could present a pyrrhic victory for Reddit if it successfully overturns the ban.

The Australian government has made this argument in its submission in the case, stating the obligations of the digital duty of care bill would “require the same action” as the social media ban legislation.

“Namely, preventing children having accounts or providing children with accounts that do not have any of the [restricted] features.”

australia.title: NSW council refuses to show world-renowned Gaza artwork over ‘unacceptable’ safety risk
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Shoalhaven council says Wall of Tears installation by Phil Buehler posed risk to staff, visitors and tenants Get our breaking ...
australia.content:
A New South Wales local council has refused to show a world-renowned artwork about children killed in Gaza after asking organisers to investigate hiring “armed guards” to counter the risk of “community conflict” over the mural.

The group, Shoalhaven Friends of Palestine, was aiming to show the Wall of Tears installation by American artist Phil Buehler at the Shoalhaven Regional Gallery in Nowra on Tuesday, following the work being exhibited around Australia, including on the front lawns of Parliament House in Canberra in September.

The massive artwork pays homage to the 18,457 children killed in Gaza between 7 October 2023 and 19 July 2025 and was first shown in New York on 29 January to coincide with the second anniversary of the death of Hind Rajab, a five-year-old left to bleed out among the bodies of six family members after their car was targeted by an Israeli tank.

Shoalhaven city council asked the group to “investigate” the use of “armed guards” in a risk assessment seen by Guardian Australia. The perceived risks included “protest, counter-protest, community conflict,” and “verbal abuse, intimidation or disruption arising from politically sensitive subject matter”.

The group was also asked to reduce the exhibition window from eight days to three days and restrict attendance to RSVPs only in the gallery, which would have “locked doors”.

Organisers were also requested to no longer advertise the event due to potential “reputational risk” for the gallery or council due to their decision to host the exhibition.

“We were like, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me,’ but we still wrote back to them and said we would meet all the requirements you want,” said Annette Pham, a member of the group.

“We didn’t even know where we could get armed guards, or if you could get them.”

Despite this, email correspondence shows Andrew Constance – the chief executive of the council and former Liberal MP – decided against hosting the event, citing staff safety concerns.

Pham wrote to the council stating she was “deeply disappointed” by the decision and said the “very suggestion that armed guards might be necessary for an exhibition commemorating dead children is deeply disturbing”.

“We are organising a memorial art exhibition, not an event for which Council has disclosed any specific credible threat of violence requiring consideration of armed protection and metal screening,” Pham wrote in her email.

A council spokesperson said in a statement that they had considered the request, but “the installation was deemed to present an unacceptable level of risk to gallery staff, visitors and tenants of the building”.

The council did not respond directly to a question from Guardian Australia about what had triggered the safety concerns.

Pham has now arranged for the work to be installed at Berry Uniting Church on Thursday.

‘They’re children’

Buehler said he was shocked his artwork, which has been shown in cities around the world, could be perceived as posing a safety risk.

“They’re children. They’re like your children, my children,” he said, adding it refers to death toll figures accepted by Israel. The artwork draws from Guardian reporting.

“If you look at the pictures on that mural … There’s kids in their little graduation outfits holding diplomas, they’re holding soccer balls. They’re there with their siblings, or on their father’s shoulder. It was the hardest artwork I’ve ever made, to just live with [what happened to these children], for the time it took to make it.”

“If people would just look at that, how can that be dangerous? The danger is put on by other people who are trying to turn it into something it’s not.”

The artwork has been touring around Australia, including in Adelaide where it was first shown, and Perth where it was shown at the Western Australian state parliament.

Dr Mairead Heaney is part of Perth Doctors Medical Aid for Palestine which helped arrange the exhibition at the WA parliament and the federal Parliament House in Canberra.

She said a number of Labor, Greens and independent MPs visited the artwork when it was displayed in Canberra, including Labor MP Tony Zappia, who made a statement to parliament about it.

Zappia said in his speech: “The banner is a sad reminder of the level of Palestinian human losses, suffering, and daily violations they endure, while much of the world looks away.”

world.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
world.snippet: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering ill...
world.content:
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.

South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.

Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.

The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.

However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.

“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.

“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

world.title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
world.snippet: Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF Members of the Sudanese ...
world.content:
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.

Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.

There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”

He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.

“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”

Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

world.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
world.snippet: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah,...
world.content:
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.

Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

world.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
world.snippet: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and pos...
world.content:
The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.

“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”

This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.

On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.

The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.

Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.

The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.

Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.

“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.

At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”

Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.

“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

world.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
world.snippet: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected t...
world.content:
Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.

A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.

The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.

The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.

Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.

A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”

During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.

The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.
